This work outlines the exterior complex scaling (ECS) methodology applied to localized and scaled-extended wave functions, addressing systems ranging from single-electron entities like atoms and ions to multi-electron configurations and multi-orbital systems such as atoms, ions, and molecules. It examines ECS signatures in total energy, density of states, ionization energies, dipole moments, and dipole polarizabilities. Additionally, it analyzes the dynamics of ionization and stimulated Raman scattering within helium atoms and hydrogen molecules exposed to DC electric fields.

We demonstrate that an augmented implementation of the Sinkhorn algorithm can always yield a convergent sequence, irrespective of whether the associated Schr\"odinger problem admits a solution. This result holds for any point mass $p_0$ and general support matrices, contrasting sharply with the classical case involving continuous measures, where convergence is guaranteed only when a solution exists. Furthermore, should the Schr\"odinger problem fail to have a solution, the limiting behavior of the algorithm's output is characterized by a specific normal form.

The cross-section for inclusive production of top quark-antiquark pairs ($t\bar{t}$) has been measured using proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 5.02$ TeV via the ATLAS detector at the LHC. Utilizing data from 2015 and 2016 corresponding to an integrated luminosity of $2.6$ fb$^{-1}$, the analysis employs the full muon, electron, and tau lepton channels. The total rate is determined to be $\sigma_{t\bar{t}} = 10.0 \pm 0.3\,(\text{stat}) \pm 0.7\,(\text{syst}) \pm 0.2\,(\text{lumi})$ pb, which aligns with standard Model predictions. Additionally, differential cross-sections were calculated as functions of the top quark pair invariant mass, transverse and longitudinal momenta, and the rapidity, with results also consistent within statistical and systematic uncertainties against Standard Model expectations.

We investigate the transition from inhomogeneous to homogeneous localization dynamics within a finite chain of quantum harmonic oscillators interacting with a central spin. Using tensor networks, we determine the asymptotic time evolution of this composite system, focusing on the interplay between the initial quantum state of the central spin and the resulting dynamics. Our numerical analysis, supported by analytical insights, examines how the invariants of motion characterizing the initial state of the central spin influence the short- and long-time behaviors of the coupled oscillators. Our results demonstrate that the initial spin state critically dictates both the transient and steady-state dynamics of the oscillators, revealing that the asymptotic configuration of the system's quantum entanglement and the time evolution of the von Neumann entropy are governed by the corresponding properties of a Hermitian operator derived from the initial conditions of the central spin.

Face detection and optical recognition of payment cards offer a robust means of examining the demographic makeup and activity patterns of metropolitan regions. This study leverages data from IDP Technologies, a global leader in facial and payment card analytics, to assess how pandemic-related behavioral shifts altered the diversity of urban encounters across income levels. The analysis reveals a decline in the variety of face-to-face interactions between individuals with different incomes, a trend that was more pronounced in major U.S. cities characterized by earlier pandemic onset and stricter containment protocols. These findings underscore the critical role of physical interaction diversity in economic resilience and recovery.

This study evaluates the performance of two non-linear field-split pre-conditioners within a two-phase flow context: the MMS approach and the recently developed NMS method. Both are applied to a nonlinear saturation-pressure solver utilizing a multigrid geometric additive algorithm. While numerical results indicate that both pre-conditioners yield comparable solutions, the MMS approach demonstrates superior speed and efficiency. Consequently, the research concludes with an implementation of this FSS method in the open-source subsurface simulator MOOSE.

This study investigates one-handedness chirality optical cavities, which are constructed using a single circularly polarized light beam interacting with a setup involving two mirrors, each set at 45° to the incident beam, arranged in parallel. This configuration demonstrates two key properties: first, the mirrors reflect incident polarization with conversion, rotating it by 90° relative to the horizontal axis when the mirror's normal is perpendicular to that direction; second, the system produces profound chemical potential asymmetry between horizontal and vertical polarizations of confined photons. Consequently, the optical mode of higher confinement experiences significantly lower energy levels, leading to a phase-to-phase transition. Furthermore, the system supports polarization-induced non-Hermitian skin effects, resulting in the accumulation of modes near the boundaries of the device. These effects are corroborated by numerical simulations and analytical models derived from these findings.

This paper explores the relationship between the two-dimensional Jackiw-Teitelboim (JT) gravity of the Schwarzschild black hole and the JT gravity limit of Liouville CFT, which is achieved by tuning the Newton's constant to approach the negative infinity. We demonstrate that the path integral of the Liouville CFT, defined over a genus-$g$ 2D surface with $n$ boundaries, converges precisely to the one-loop partition function of $JT$ gravity on the same topological setup. This equivalence holds for a Newton's constant that depends explicitly on the number of boundaries ($n$) and satisfies the asymptotic condition of tending towards negative infinity. Furthermore, we establish that the matrix model of Gao and Maxfield emerges in the asymptotic limit of Liouville CFT under these same constraints.

The Alcubierre metric can be adapted to accommodate a non-zero value for the cosmological constant. In this modified framework, incorporating a cosmological constant necessitates an additional massless field to sustain the warp bubble, whereas a non-zero cosmological constant allows a matter distribution with a negative specific relativistic energy density to drive the acceleration. This mechanism enables solutions for the warp drive using both massless fluids and perfect fluids with a negative equation of state. Notably, these warp drive configurations can be realized with the inclusion of either a massless or imperfect cosmological constant cosmology.

This work outlines the guidelines for the GD-3C project, specifically addressing Geospatial Urban Infrastructure Data Engineering Solutions (GUIDES). The primary aim is to develop guidelines, best practices, and case studies for the data engineering processes involved in managing large-scale geospatial references for urban infrastructure. The resulting document is intended to assist professionals, stakeholders, and experts in the urban infrastructure domain who engage with Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and Digital Twin technologies.

Tip-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy (TERS) is a highly promising spectroscopic technique that delivers both superior spatial resolution and enhanced sensitivity. Nevertheless, extracting precise information regarding the chemical and electromagnetic enhancements from TERS data remains difficult. This study presents a fully quantum mechanical investigation of a tip-surface system subjected to electromagnetic and chemical interactions. By applying the Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory (TD-DFT) method, we calculated the excitation energies of the system under various gap potentials representing chemical and electromagnetic effects separately. Our results indicate that distinct spatial distributions emerge between the electromagnetic and chemical effects, with electromagnetic contributions showing a significantly broader range compared to chemical effects. Consequently, these findings enable the quantitative separation of these two factors based on TERS data.

Ammonium sulfate is a unique material that displays both proton and dipolar ferroelectricity, characterized by a distinct switching of ferroelectric domains at their respective phase transitions. This study investigates the entropy variations associated with these transitions in ammonium sulfate, revealing that the entropy change linked with the caloric transition driven by dipolar moments is significantly greater than that driven by proton moments. This observation contradicts prior theories, which anticipated that the entropy change would correlate with the magnitude of the dipole moment. Instead, our results reveal that the entropy change is proportional to the expansion of the unit cell volume during the transition. This phenomenon is attributed to the extensive liberation of rotational freedom experienced by the dipolar molecules as transition occurs. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that the entropy change for any given transition is determined by the volume of the unit cell resulting from the high-temperature symmetry, rather than the size of the dipole moment involved. This insight offers a comprehensive understanding of the thermodynamics underlying ammonium sulfate's phase transitions and establishes a dependable framework for investigating other entropy-driven calorics transitions.

Reinforcement learning (RL) theories describe how the brain learns to navigate complex, uncertain environments by updating action values based on reward prediction errors. While theoretical models suggest that individual differences in these learned strategies may be adaptive, our findings indicate that specific variations—such as those in dopamine sensitivity, exploration tendencies, and discount rates—are consistently associated with neural activity in the midbrain. Using a novel midfMRI midbrain segmentation method, our results reveal a shared pattern of neural engagement for distinct behavioral traits, suggesting that the midbrain responds to the magnitude of reward prediction errors regardless of whether an individual's strategy is optimal or suboptimal. This neural flexibility appears to account for the stability of these behavioral strategies across diverse situations, indicating that the brain tracks multiple, simultaneously active processes.

This work addresses the $c$-approximate and $\epsilon$-approximate $k$-near-neighbor problems under the Fréchet distance for vertex-aligned and Fréchet-bounded simple polygons with $n$ vertices, where queries consist of $q$-vertex polygons. We present new algorithms with running times of $\mathsf{cANNS}$ $\tilde{O}(n^{1-1/q})$ and $\mathsf{eANNS}$ $\tilde{O}((nq)^{1-1/\epsilon})$, respectively, alongside approximate bounds. These results are optimal to within constant factors when $q$ is small (i.e., $q \le n/2$) and provide improved performance guarantees compared to previous work for larger values of $q$. The paper also establishes a lower bound of $\Omega(n^{1-\Omega(1/q)})$ for any algorithm solving either problem type, which is tight up to constant factors for scenarios where $q$ exceeds $n/2$. Additionally, we introduce a generic framework for constructing a $c$-approximate Fréchet distance label set with size $\tilde{O}(n^{1-1/q})$ and can be computed in $\tilde{O}(nq^2)$ time. Measurement Error Mitigation (MEM) addresses systematic measurement biases prevalent in contemporary quantum hardware. While techniques like Probabilistic Calibration (calPROB) and Vector Rescaling (calVEC) have been established, they face limitations in resource demands or mitigation effectiveness. We introduce an Iteration MEM (iterMEM) approach, a general iterative framework capable of refining existing MEM methods such as calPROB and calVEC. Specifically, we demonstrate the Iteration MEM (calPROB) variant, which offers analytical expressions for updating calibration matrices and provide practical guidance for its convergence behavior. Experimental results from two- and three-qubit Grover's algorithm runs on IBM quantum processors reveal that iterMEM-enhanced calPROB significantly reduces outcome variance compared to standard implementations, outperforming standard methods by a wide margin.

To successfully negotiate tasks, adapt to human teammates, and effectively demonstrate intentions in dynamic environments, robots must communicate their internal states to people. While robots can perform self-localization and self-assessment independently, conveying this information to humans is essential for facilitating task negotiation and shared autonomy. This paper introduces a technique to teach robots the capability to communicate their conventions through experiences of being controlled by humans. In our study, humans were asked to guide robots to reach specific goals and avoid obstacles during a series of trials. The results indicate that the robots developed the ability to convey the level of their autonomy to the human controller based on their confidence levels. The study also shows that these robots can successfully execute tasks even when their human operators are absent.

Autonomous navigation within unfamiliar environments remains a persistent challenge for mobile robots. While current approaches predominantly utilize metric or grid-based maps, they often struggle with issues such as high memory consumption, computational inefficiency, and localization ambiguity. To address these limitations, this paper introduces HiTMap, a hierarchical topological representation designed to facilitate robust exploration and recovery. The framework consists of two main components: a global map and a local navigational model. Global representation relies on hierarchical topological graph elements to effectively manage vast spaces, whereas navigation is guided by a dual-laser system that infers motion through a sequence prediction framework. Both components work in concert, allowing the robot to transition efficiently between detailed metric zones and coarse topological representations. Experimental results from simulated environments demonstrate that HiTMap successfully reduces metric map reliance and enhances performance in terms of accuracy, speed, and memory usage compared to prior techniques.

This study introduces novel methods for building code sets with inter-group complementary code (ICCS) and two-dimensional Z-complementary array code (CZACs) utilizing multivariable functions. Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively used in medical diagnostics, but standard single-energy CT often lacks sufficient tissue characterization for critical applications like radiation therapy planning. Employing a polychromatic source with a multi-energy approach offers a promising solution to overcome this limitation. However, acquiring X-ray data across numerous energy levels necessitates a high sensor count, which can be costly and slow, thereby restricting its practicality. To address these constraints, this paper introduces an innovative experimental framework designed to minimize the required number of sensors while enhancing reconstruction quality. By utilizing a shared readout device paired with polyenergetic illumination, the study demonstrates that by manipulating the input X-ray intensity at a single sensor, researchers can virtually probe multiple energy levels. This allows for multi-energy reconstructions that surpass the resolution and accuracy achievable with single-energy CT. Furthermore, the data can be decomposed into its constituent material compositions. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first experimental study to successfully implement multi-energy reconstruction and material decomposition using polyenerization with a single shared sensor. Validated by a multi-energy reconstruction and decomposition pipeline, the results are processed through a new variational model that jointly handles image reconstruction, sensor denoising, and material decomposition. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated on real multi-energy datasets, with quantitative and visual results confirming its effectiveness.

We investigate how light propagates across a vacuum gap separating two metallic surfaces, focusing on the impacts of electron spill-out and nonlocal response. Specifically, we examine the case where the physical gap thickness is smaller than the range of these effects. By utilizing both a phenomenological model and a formal treatment based on the random phase approximation, we demonstrate that both spill-out and electron electron dynamics consistently lead to a reduced nonlocal range in the presence of a low-energy surface plasmon-polariton (gap-plasmon). This phenomenon is attributed to the collective influence of both surface plasmons and dynamical electrostatic screening. Our findings indicate that the extent of spill-out and nonlocal characteristics is governed by the average electron density in the region encompassing the vacuum space and the two metals. This work provides essential guidance for investigating the quantum behaviors of surface plasmon-polaritons in extremely confined geometries.

This paper examines the influence of relevance feedback on results obtained from contextual named entity retrieval. We introduce a term-based feedback method that leverages user interaction to adjust search queries. Empirical findings indicate that this approach outperforms a baseline that relies solely on initial user input, while also exceeding a document-centric feedback method.

Time series datasets, characterized by sequential data points collected at regular intervals, are essential for understanding dynamic processes. While tools exist for visualizing them, interactivity remains crucial for examining details, particularly in complex multivariate forms. This paper introduces a new set of interaction techniques that leverage visual change to explain data transformations. Our approach includes three core gestures: the first highlights specific series by gradually fading others, the second reveals specific values by expanding them, and the third merges multiple series by adaptively adjusting their lengths. Users can employ these techniques individually or in combination to access intricate data features. We tested our methods on three data sets of varying complexity, gathering both quantitative and qualitative feedback. Results indicate that all techniques improve user performance and satisfaction compared to standard interface controls.

Mining patient health records from vast Electronic Health Record (EHR) systems has become a vital necessity for advancing precision medicine and tailoring treatments. To address this, the paper introduces Heterogeneous Similar Graph Neural Networks (HetSimGNN), a specialized model designed to identify patient cohorts with comparable clinical histories. HetSimGNN accounts for the unique characteristics of EHRs, including their multi-modal nature, sparse distribution, and significant imbalance. The architecture integrates both graph-based and matrix-based mechanisms to capture diverse relationships among patient attributes. It constructs interaction graphs for patients and their associated attributes, utilizing Graph Neural Networks to refine representations, while also employing low-rank matrix factorization on the graph-derived node embeddings. The proposed method was evaluated on an EHR dataset from MGH Boston using three distinct downstream tasks: patient similarity estimation, patient classification, and patient clustering. The results demonstrate that HetSimGNN significantly surpasses existing approaches across all metrics.

This study investigates how local solvent polarization affects the electric double layer (EDL) near a charged soft surface within an electrolyte solution using the Poisson-Boltzmann framework. By developing a local dielectric model where the solvent's dielectric constant decreases linearly with increasing polymer volume fraction, we found that surface solvent polarization significantly influences EDL structure. Compared to the standard constant dielectric approximation, it leads to a thinner double layer characterized by higher surface potentials and an enhanced charge density within the polymeric region. Furthermore, when comparing predictions against the classic constant dielectric Poisson-Boltzmann solutions, the model incorporating variable dielectric constants accurately reproduces the steric compression effects observed in a traditional theory that explicitly includes finite ion size limitations.

This study investigates the energy-efficient cooperative network coding (ECNC) problem within a multi-relay network. The goal is to minimize the total transmit power of all relays while adhering to a predefined outage probability threshold. To address this, a joint relay scheduling and power allocation (JRSAP) framework is introduced. The resulting problem is first transformed into an equivalent form that separates variables, which is then further converted into an optimization task focused on power allocation among relays. A new iterative algorithm based on bisection search is proposed to resolve this task. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the proposed ECNC strategy surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques in energy efficiency.

This study investigates magnetic impurities situated on a superconducting surface using first-principles methods. We examine a Mn atom and two distinct configurations of Mn dimers on Nb(110), employing the fully-relativistic, fully-polarized linearized augmented plane-wave (LAPW) method. Our analysis reveals that the magnetic moments of these impurities are driven by two components: first, the formation of a narrow, highly impurity-localized $d$-band situated within the Nb host's $p$-band gap, and second, the spin polarization of Nb $d$-states extending into the energy gap. We calculate the zero-temperature spin-up and spin-down density of states (DOS) for Nb to determine the Yu-Shiba-Rusinov resonance positions, observing that these values align well with recent experimental findings. We also evaluate the DOS contributions from both the Nb environment and the Mn impurities, finding that although DOS from the $s$ and $p$ bands of Nb is significant, the primary source of DOS in the gap originates from the $d$ bands of the impurity atom. Additionally, we explore the relationship between the $g$-factor and the strength of the exchange coupling parameter ($\alpha$) for the impurity's $d$ orbital, finding that this relationship is non-monotonic. We also provide a detailed analysis of the orbital composition of the $g$-factors.

This study introduces a novel experimental strategy for investigating the rare decay $K^+\rightarrow\pi^+\nu\bar{\nu}$ utilizing a decay-in-flight methodology. The analysis relies on data collected by the PANDA experiment at FAIR, utilizing 1.1 $\times$ 10$^{32}$ nucleon-nucleon on-target yields acquired during the run-up to hadronic investigations. By focusing on a $K^+$ beam with momentum of 1.9 GeV/$c$, the study establishes a 90% confidence-level lower limit of $3.9 \times$ 10$^{-12}$ on the partial decay width, thereby surpassing the previous most sensitive result obtained at CERN. This advancement stems directly from the experiment's high-rate detection of high-intensity kaon beams and its exceptional resolution for identifying neutral particles.

Distribution-to-distribution registration is widely used for aligning 3D point clouds, relying on the best-matching principle where distributions are registered by optimally selecting corresponding points. However, when point clouds contain significant noise, this approach produces suboptimal registration accuracy. This paper introduces a novel Deep Neural Network (DNN)-based filter designed to mitigate noise within the distribution utilized during the optimization of distribution-level registration tasks. By applying this filtering technique, we achieve more precise point-to-point alignment across the registered distributions. Experimental evaluations were conducted across three distinct noise scenarios to validate the filter's efficacy. Results indicate that the proposed method achieves superior bias reduction across all tested noise levels.

Satellite imagery offers a comprehensive view of the landscape, enabling various applications ranging from medical and agricultural uses to security and defense. While current satellite technology captures images with exceptional clarity, the vast volume of available data makes it difficult to manually identify objects of interest. This paper introduces a novel network architecture that achieves accurate edge detection using standard 24-bit RGB input without relying on deep learning. The method is validated on two distinct satellite datasets, demonstrating that it outperforms several existing non-deep-learning-based edge detectors.

Utilizing a straightforward rate-based framework, we examine the time- and frequency-domain characteristics of non-linear X-ray absorption near-edge absorption (XANES) spectra, which emerge when X-ray pulses are intense enough to drive rapid electron excitations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that non-linear X-ray absorption can be modeled as a convolution of the linear cross-section with the electron excitation rate. These findings are validated by comparing our theoretical predictions with results from rate-model simulations and time-resolved experiments.

Massive star formation occurs in a cyclical process where protostellar feedback compresses molecular gas, triggering the formation of subsequent stars. While this mechanism is well-understood in simpler, single-cycle contexts, its complexity increases in environments containing multiple compressed filaments and dark clouds. This study investigates the Dragon infrared dark cloud (IC 5146B), a system comprising four parallel filaments and three distinct dark clouds, to determine if core growth aligns with the core-to-cloud mass ratio (CMR) evolution predicted by core growth models. We analyzed CMR development across three epochs of 10 years each using sub-100 $\mu$m data from the Herschel Space Observatory. Our findings indicate that core growth is occurring within the cloud, specifically in regions of dense cores located between parallel filaments. Consequently, core growth is confirmed in a complex multi-filament setting, providing robust support for the core growth model even in such intricate star-forming complexes.

This study examines a series of well-characterized glass-forming polymers to establish universal trends correlating dynamic and thermodynamic non-ergodicity. Recent breakthroughs in transformer-based models have spurred significant research into their ability to process negation, with many studies highlighting deficiencies in handling negated statements. Our results indicate that transformer models struggle significantly more with negative items from the advanced cognitive domain than with positive controls, thereby demonstrating both a deficit in current transformer architectures and alignment with findings from human studies on negation proficiency.

Specifically, we integrate this mechanism into the self-attention layer of the decoder alongside an adaptive strategy that dynamically adjusts the maximum look-ahead window size. Experiments across multiple public datasets demonstrate that our method significantly enhances translation quality, particularly for out-of-vocabulary terms, long dependencies, and specialized domains. We present a new analysis of diffuse gamma-ray emission from galaxy clusters, utilizing both observational data and theoretical modeling. This work features a re-evaluation of the background gamma-ray flux in the energy range of 100 MeV to 10 GeV, specifically for regions surrounding galaxy clusters. We argue that current uncertainties in the background flux levels hinder the detection of signals from clusters and significantly hamper the ability to interpret and interpret potential future observations. We illustrate our approach by analyzing observations of the Coma Cluster across various energy bands, demonstrating that the current instrumental sensitivity is insufficient to detect either the dark matter annihilation or decay signals, nor can it constrain these processes effectively. Furthermore, we examine the correlation between the observed background and cluster properties, such as luminosity and redshift, to define the future observational thresholds necessary to identify dark matter signatures from individual clusters or galaxy groups. We also assess the potential of upcoming instruments, such as the upgraded Fermi mission, the Cosmic Gamma-ray Space Telescope (COSI), and the Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA), to detect dark matter annihilation in Coma. Additionally, we explore the hypothesis that the background gamma-ray flux originates from starburst galaxies and active galactic nuclei (AGN), analyzing both their correlations with cluster characteristics and their capability to set limits on dark matter models.

Features in the primordial power spectrum can generate oscillations in the primordial tensor mode spectrum. Although the frequency of these oscillations is established by the sound horizon at a specific early epoch, our ability to measure them hinges on the physical mechanism responsible. We explore how a classical cosmological collider operating during inflation produces these oscillations. In this scenario, heavy particles interact with a primordial gravitational field, resulting in correlated interactions between different modes. These correlations are imprinted as an initial tensor mode oscillation, which persists throughout subsequent evolution. A classical collider operating at inflation could thus be identified through its unique signature: the resulting tensor mode power spectrum would display scale-dependent variations tied to the ratios of wavenumbers to the early sound horizon frequency. Finally, we explore several early universe scenarios that could function as a classical cosmological collider.

Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are essential for solving key computer vision tasks, such as classification, detection, and semantic segmentation. However, their performance is difficult to interpret. This study presents a new method to analyze convolutional filters within these networks. We introduce a visual-semantic framework designed to elucidate the function of each filter by examining the relationship between its input latent features and output activations. Experimentally, our proposed Latent Visual-semantc Filter Attention (LVFA) network is used to train a network that captures these interactions. Our results demonstrate two main advantages: first, our method offers greater interpretability by visualizing intermediate layers alongside semantic annotations, and second, it is effective at enhancing accuracy. Specifically, retraining the COCO dataset using this network increased Pascal VOC and Pascal VOC-LVF performance by 1.3% and 0.7%, respectively.

This paper investigates the role of longitudinal phonons in a single-chain cuprate model characterized by Coulomb repulsion, nearest-neighbor attraction, and electron-phonon coupling. While the mean-field approximation suggests that nearest-neighbor attraction alone is insufficient to generate bound pairs unlike in BCS theory, our findings indicate that coupling to longitudinal phonons mediates a significant attractive force over long ranges, facilitating formation of electron pairs.

The MPHIA study, a 10-year prospective cohort design, investigates the associations between lifestyle and environmental factors and the development of hypertension, coronary heart disease, stroke, cancer, and chronic kidney disease. This paper details the structural causal model (SCM) construction for the study, which relies on data from 10,602 participants collected via interviews and examinations. An influence diagram was initially developed to represent the observed data-generating process, followed by the construction of a Causal Structure Model using a local scoring method. This approach was applied to a dataset comprising 10 observed and one latent variable. Analysis yielded a SCMs with 21 distinct causal influences, including bidirectional effects between age and obesity, as well as unidirectional effects where obesity influences stroke risk.

The chiral magnet Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ features a magnetic skyrmion lattice (SkL) state situated between temperatures of 150 mK and 10 K, which forms via a second-order phase transition. This material also supports metastable SkL states that can be accessed by applying a magnetic field. In this study, we utilize high-resolution neutron diffraction to examine the evolution of this field-induced metastable regime as it melts at temperatures below 10 mK. Our findings reveal that the transition from the magnetically disordered state to the set of discrete reflections defining the SkL occurs in two distinct steps. The emergence of the first partial reflection set happens at a specific field threshold, $B_c$, coinciding with the magnetization of the uniform phase. Subsequently, the remaining SkL reflections appear only after the full transition to a hexagonal SkL state is completed. These results indicate that the melting process reorganizes the originally metastable lattice into a thermodynamically stable one. Furthermore, we observe that the field-induced phase transition displays clear signs of critical slowing down.

The Nikaidô-Isoda-Fan inequality defines an equilibrium problem (EP), for which numerous researchers in optimization have sought solutions. In this study, fixed points of certain mappings are demonstrated to align with the solutions of EP. Leveraging this connection, the authors introduce the nearest point projection algorithm to identify an arbitrary approximate fixed point and apply it to EP to establish the existence proof for an efficient and effective method. Recent research has demonstrated that Large Language Models (LLMs) and similar deep learning systems are susceptible to concealing binary-bit messages within their weights, recoverable via the application of specialized steganographic neural networks (NNs). Notably, these messages remain undetectable by human evaluators of the affected models. Addressing the challenge of creating reversible steganography in neural networks, we introduce a method to render these hidden messages recoverable. Rather than a traditional steganographic approach, we train a specific neural network to locate model weights that bear an explicit signature of an embedded message. Utilizing maximum likelihood estimation and Bayesian principles, this framework identifies the statistical likelihood of message bits and simultaneously determines the degree of certainty regarding their status. Empirical results indicate that, relative to existing methods, our approach achieves a 100% success rate in accurately decoding the information content of trained LLMs, while maintaining performance levels for generative tasks comparable to those of standard (non-reversible) embedding techniques.

To determine the suitability of mean-field models for examining global dynamo mechanisms, we conducted simulations of periodic, turbulent convection within rapidly rotating stratified spheres. These experiments utilized the incompressible, anisotropic Navier-Stokes equations and the thermal energy conservation law, driven by a time-dependent bottom heat flux. Our findings indicate that turbulent dynamos can emerge across both the radiative and the overlying adiabatic regimes. By comparing the time-averaged magnetic field spectra between the two cases, we observed that the dynamo in the radiative regime produced significantly stronger mean fields than in the adiabatic regime. This difference suggests that turbulent convection effects are strongly dependent on the boundary conditions. Specifically, we identified that the overlying adiabatic regions act as reservoirs of free magnetic helicity, thereby driving a more efficient dynamo in the underlying radiative zone. Accurate detection of inter-beat intervals (IBIs) is vital for biomedicine, particularly in the analysis of cardiovascular dynamics and beat-to-beat oxygenation. Calibrating an eye-in-hand camera is a fundamental requirement for robotics, yet it frequently proves difficult to execute due to the labor-intensive nature of traditional methods. Our research proposes a novel approach to model the extrinsic parameters of a robot manipulator holding a camera by utilizing their known structure and a single image. Our method is grounded in the geometric relationship between the camera's principal point and its projection of the manipulator structure. Leveraging the invariance of these projections to projectors, our approach modelsthe relationship as a quadratic one between a set of quadratic curves observed within the image. The method yields two algebraic equations containing the coupled extrinsic and intrinsic parameters; our solution strategy prioritizes estimating the extrinsic parameters by approximating the intrinsic parameters using a pre-determined camera model. Finally, intrinsic parameters are refined via an iterative process, utilizing an image-based approach to ensure the eye-in-hand calibration is supported by accurate extrinsic data. Our approach is demonstrated on simulated data as well as real-world images captured by various sensors, including RGB and RGB-D units.

Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) seeks to identify an unknown reward function that is consistent with the demonstrated behavior of an expert. This problem is often modeled as finding a single reward function whose corresponding optimal policy, within some given class, is compatible with the expert's observations. This article establishes that when the reward function class is *fully observable* to the IRL agent, IRL can be recast as an optimization task. We demonstrate this for two scenarios: when demonstrated trajectories are *best-case* (optimal) for the expert, or when they are *arbitrary* (non-optimal). In both cases, we provide an explicit optimization formulation that includes constraints and show the computational complexity of solving these problems. We also present specific examples illustrating how to construct IRL optimization frameworks using observable rewards. These findings lay the groundwork for investigating how agent capabilities vary based on IRL settings and the information available to the agent.

GAIA is designed to create an unparalleled 3D map of our galaxy's structure and kinematics. By targeting over 1 billion stars, the mission will deliver the most precise astrometric data available to date. The endeavor is led by ESA, with the initial launch scheduled for late 2013; a significant update to the data release is planned for 2023. This article will detail the scientific objectives, technical specifications, and operational framework of the project. Furthermore, it will highlight the pioneering 3D mapping techniques of our local stellar populations and the innovative approaches to stellar astrophysics enabled by GAIA's unique capabilities. Finally, the discussion will address upcoming scientific frontiers, including the study of the Sun's formation history, heliospheric dynamics, and the stellar architecture of the Galaxy. Special attention will also be given to the stellar evolution and internal physics of the young, metal-rich stars found in the solar neighborhood, as well as the structural and dynamical characteristics of the Galactic disc.

For an $n$-vertex graph, the task of vertex separators for treewidth seeks an integer $k$ and subset $S$ such that removing $S$ disconnects the graph into components with at most $k$ vertices each, under a constraint that $|S|$ remains sublinear. This research establishes that sublinear space is sufficient for this problem. Our approach involves two primary components. First, we present a linear-time, sublinear-space algorithm to compute a treewidth approximation. Second, we introduce a novel technique to find treewidth solutions in space efficiency by adapting the separation of problems into smaller subproblems. These contributions not only resolve the existence of such separators but also advance understanding in related fields, specifically minor-free graphs and the selection committee problem.

We introduce a broadened definition of directed clustering, a method previously confined to homogeneous, undirected networks. Our approach integrates three specific network characteristics: asymmetry, weights, and the distinction between measured and inferred links. As a generalization of weighted undirected clustering, our framework utilizes silhouette scores to evaluate cluster quality. This method is flexible enough to accommodate networks that are either measured or inferred; specifically, we define three novel silhouette metrics that account for the unique properties of known and suspected ties. These extensions allow researchers to analyze inferred networks that are often mistakenly treated as measured. By accounting for asymmetry and the probabilities of missing or spurious ties, our framework ensures that the structural biases inherent in inferred networks are not erroneously interpreted as meaningful patterns. Furthermore, we operationalize this conceptual model through three distinct metric sets: (1) `inferred ties`, designed to handle the probability of spurious links and the probability of missing links, (2) `link asymmetry ties`, which evaluates the quality of clusters by considering the strength of these ties and the strength of the absence of these ties; and (3) `inferred ties`, which evaluates the quality of clusters by considering the strength of these ties and the strength of the absence of these ties. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have established themselves as a powerful tool for resolving partial differential equations (PDEs) by integrating physical laws into machine learning. However, like most artificial neural networks, PINNs lack a theoretical framework to estimate their training errors. Drawing inspiration from finite element methods, this study develops a reliable and post-hoc error estimation technique for PINNs. The methodology involves solving local error estimates on small sub-regions within the domain to generate global error bounds, thereby providing solid grounds for the certification of PINNs' predictive capabilities. The validity and efficacy of this approach are validated across two distinct PDE scenarios, including the Poisson and Helmholtz equations.

A critical challenge in epidemiological research is the precise characterization of air pollution exposure. This work reviews recent advancements in these field, highlighting the integration of geostatistics and machine learning within air pollution modeling. The discussion begins by examining temporal and spatial patterns in air pollution, followed by an exploration of models that integrate remote sensing, chemical transport, and meteorological data. A key focus is placed on spatio-temporal estimation techniques utilizing geostatistics and machine learning. An air pollution dataset, along with the corresponding R code for reproducible analysis, can be found in this repository: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3852415.

This study introduces a tunneling spectroscopy method designed to distinguish Majorana zero-energy peaks from trivial ones by utilizing an asymmetric junction where a superconductor is replaced with a normal metal exhibiting the Kondo effect. We developed a theoretical framework to derive the junction's differential conductance spectrum and found that the Majorana peak is uniquely identified by a constant, frequency-independent Majorana fermion-dissipation relationship. In contrast, the trivial peak displays a frequency-dependent response that scales with the applied voltage. These findings offer a straightforward and effective pathway for both identifying and isolating Majorana modes within topological systems.

Adversarial machine learning is a relatively young field that examines how malicious actors exploit models to degrade performance, compromise model integrity, or cause data misclassification. While extensive research has focused on models like Support Vector Machines and neural networks, graph neural networks (GNNs)—which are increasingly prevalent in the data science community—remain largely unexplored in terms of adversarial attacks. This gap exists despite the fact that GNNs are highly susceptible to data poisoning attacks. This paper investigates how limited and noisy label information affects the efficacy of data poisoning strategies within GNNs. We present a reinforcement learning approach designed to execute poisoning attacks on graphs, capable of navigating the complex, high-dimensional state space inherent to graph structures. Our findings demonstrate that this method achieves superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art techniques.

The primary function of astrometric catalogs is to compile data on celestial object positions, proper motions, and photometry, which facilitates the identification of common astrometric and photometric signatures to cross-match catalogues. While astrometry is essential, photometric parameters are equally critical for verifying physical associations between objects. This study proposes a new photometric matching technique that leverages photometric features to enhance the accuracy of catalogue matching. The algorithm utilizes the photometric parameters $U-G$, $G$, and $r-p_c$ derived from the Gaia EDR3 Release 3 catalogues. The performance of this new method is assessed using two approaches: (1) cross-matching Gaia EDR3 with the Pan-STARRY1 photometric catalog, and 2) cross-matching Gaia EDR3 with the 2MASS photometric catalog. The results indicate that incorporating photometric parameters significantly improves cross-matching precision compared to relying solely on astrometry.

Ontologies serve as a formal means to define concepts and their interconnections, making them crucial for creating shared understanding among diverse groups. While existing visualization methods are effective for small-scale datasets, they struggle with large ontologies due to issues such as: (i) hierarchical structures hindering the view of non-hierarchical relations; (ii) layout instability upon interaction, requiring repeated re-arrangement after every change; and (iii) an inability to distinguish ontological categories. To address these challenges, we introduce **OntoPlot**, a new visualization tool that allows users to view all relationships within an ontology and supports interactive navigation. Key features include the capability to display multiple categories and filter ontology types, dynamically showing item counts per group. Furthermore, users can see associated concepts and properties for specific entities without needing to close or modify open options. Empirical testing indicates that entities are correctly identified in 98% of cases and categorized with 96% accuracy.

This paper presents CycleGAN and an inter-domain loss approach for improving semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition (ASR). Utilizing a discriminator within a framework of three shared models and two distinct domains, our method performs image translation and image matching across these areas. Using a Korean speech dataset, experimental results indicate that employing only CycleGAN yields no performance gains. However, integrating CycleGAN with the proposed inter-domain losses leads to a reduction in Word Error Rate (WERT) of 0.7% in a fully-supervised setting and an improvement of 0.1% in the semi-supervised setting.

This study introduces a framework for model-based, goal-directed learning in artificial intelligence, rooted in the principle of active inference. Unlike the original approach, which demands manual specification of priors and requires extensive tuning by experts, our method employs a hybrid architecture combining the Bounded Shortest Path (BSP) algorithm with the Q-Learning method. This integration allows agents to acquire new behavioral repertoires by adapting their transition and reward functions through experience, rather than relying on pre-defined prior knowledge. The effectiveness of this strategy was validated via autonomous navigation tests in real-world environments using a Turtlebot3 robot, demonstrating that the agents successfully acquired navigation skills with minimal parameter adjustment. Additionally, the paper outlines a pathway for future research focused on refining the framework's efficiency by optimizing its sample complexity.

Molecular orientation is central to the Soret effect, which describes how a temperature gradient drives solute segregation in binary fluid mixtures. This study focuses on molecular softness and its impact on Soret efficiency, specifically examining how the molecular polarizability influences orientation. We constructed a Tetratopic Model (TM) featuring temperature-dependent interaction softness to explore how internal degrees of freedom affect transport. Our findings indicate that soft molecules exhibit reduced Soret efficiency compared to their rigid counterparts. Furthermore, we identified that this reduction stems primarily from the molecular polarizability hindering polar alignment rather than the internal degree of freedom itself. These results were validated using ensemble and molecular dynamics simulations, which revealed that soft molecules possess a more disordered structure and lower orientational order than rigid molecules. Crucially, our analysis demonstrated that increasing molecular polarizability weakens the dipole interaction, thereby diminishing both local molecular ordering and macroscopic solute segregation.

Automated Essay Scoring (AES) is a pivotal application of Natural Language Processing (NLP) in Education, a field that has recently seen a resurgence in NLP-driven advancements. This study investigates AES using state-of-the-art Transformer-based language models, specifically BERT and RoBERTa, comparing their efficacy against other well-established Transformer architectures like BART and, specifically, the original author's baseline, which utilized the Multilingual BART (MuLg) model. The research explores the impact of hyperparameter tuning on these architectures, comparing the performance of RoBERTa and BART. Contrary to expectations, RoBERTa demonstrated superior efficacy in generating accurate essay scores compared to the baseline, achieving an improvement of approximately 0.2 on the Pearson's correlation coefficient metric.

While supervised domain adaptive pedestrian detection has made substantial progress, it remains heavily reliant on false positive (FP) caused by clutter background. Current methods, including the standard SIAM-RCNN, fail to effectively address these clutter-induced FPs, particularly when shifting domains. This work introduces an unsupervised "Box Re-Ranking" approach to suppress FPs without requiring any re-labeling of clutter. By re-evaluating all ranked proposals, the proposed method assesses the reliability of boxes originally generated by the ranking system. Empirical results demonstrate that our unsupervised re-ranking mechanism significantly outperforms existing self-training and data augmentation strategies in eliminating false detections.

We introduce an approach designed to boost the clarity and quality of low-fidelity music tracks by employing a convolutional neural network to execute image translation. In this framework, music recordings are treated as visual images, while the neural network applies a convolutional architecture to emulate the process of converting between low and high fidelity audio states. A key advantage of this model is its ability to function effectively even when dealing with very short music excerpts. Additionally, the system integrates the system with a spectral gapper, a tool commonly used for boosting specific sound frequencies, resulting to a further enhancement across a wide range of audio bands. Tests conducted on both audio and visual metrics indicate that the proposed hybrid technique outperforms existing solutions both in fidelity and clarity.

The ability to accurately and effectively manipulate objects is fundamental to all humans, yet individuals with visual impairments often face significant difficulties due to a lack of precise feedback when object manipulation skills are needed. While current solutions exist, they often fail to address these specific needs adequately. To tackle this, we introduce FauxThrow, an assistive technology that helps people with visual challenges perform throwing tasks by providing auditory and vibrotactile cues regarding the trajectory and intended target. Users interact with this system through a hand-mounted inertial sensor that feeds real-time data on how object trajectories diverge from the plan. Experiments involving 12 participants with varying levels of vision demonstrated that FauxThrow allows for significantly more precise and effective throws compared to unaided methods. The results indicate that this technology holds promise for expanding the capabilities of individuals with visual impairments in object manipulation.

Neural machine translation (NMT) has achieved significant success in generating fluent and semantically accurate translations. However, since these systems typically rely on a greedy approach to select the highest probability child nodes during decoding, they produce right-branching parse trees that often contain syntactic errors. In response, this paper introduces a top-down, syntax-aware, constrained decoding framework designed to produce structurally correct and improved sentences. By integrating syntactic constraints and leveraging attention mechanisms to focus on relevant context, the model effectively mitigates right-branching issues. Evaluations on the Penn Treebank demonstrate a reduction in unsatisfied constraints and improvements in parsing accuracy. Applied to the WMT 19 English-German track, the framework yields an improvement of 0.2 points in BLEU under fixed parse constraints and 0.1 points in unsupervised settings.

Accurate modeling of astrochemical processes in the interstellar medium (ISI) relies heavily on precise binding energies for molecules adsorbing onto grain surfaces. These energies are critical for determining key processes such as molecular formation, surface mobility, and desorption. While quantum chemistry is an essential tool for calculating these values, the sheer volume of accessible calculations presents a significant challenge in filtering high-quality results amidst subpar work. To address this need, we introduce the Binding Energy Evaluation Platform (BEEP), an open-access database featuring a specialized evaluation tool. This tool calculates binding energies for molecular pairs on a variety of grain models using density functional theory (DFT), concurrently assessing their quality through single-point corrections and correction schemes for basis set superposition error (BSSE). The initial release of BEEP populates this database with 3000 binding energies across 100 distinct chemical combinations involving small molecules and solids, utilizing three different grain models grounded in experimental data.

This research examines a type of stochastic multiplicative process that is confined by a data-driven lower bound exhibiting exponential growth. The analysis covers both the discrete and continuous formulations of the model and derives its closed-form solutions. The application of this process proves useful in capturing the dynamic evolution of real-world asset returns, which are subject to a floor representing the cumulative value of a portfolio's cash components. The methodology is implemented using the shares of Apple Inc., where the stochastic component represents the stock's market value and the multiplicative lower bound represents the value of the associated cash holdings.

This work introduces a novel algorithm for estimating expectation values of individual terms within Hermitian operators via random circuit sampling. Unlike most contemporary approaches, it employs a quantum circuit composed of random, shallow layers of $Z$-only Clifford gates rather than deep circuits involving individual qubit access. Under the assumption that the underlying operators exhibit non-degeneracy, the proposed method remains comparable in efficiency state-of-the-art "classical" techniques, which rely on repeated measurements across standard basis states. Notably, the practical utility of the protocol extends to scenarios where an adversary controls the tested device, provided they are restricted to operations involving only a single qubit at a time. This robustness against a specific class of local quantum attacks positions the algorithm as a valuable component within the broader quantum computing security framework.

While deep learning has recently achieved significant success in natural language processing, it remains highly sensitive to hyperparameter configurations and the specific architecture selected, often resulting in sub-optimal performance. This study introduces an ensemble-based deep learning framework designed to enhance the robustness of text classification models. The method leverages Sybil Variants Transformations, which utilize character-level operations to generate augmented data and diverse sets of robustness ensembles. These include an intra-ensemble formed by applying Sybil Variants to training samples and an inter-ensemble created by directing various character-level and cluster-level operations onto the transformed data within the same pipeline. Classification is determined through a democratic vote aggregating predictions from both the Sybil-Transformed intra-ensemble and the transformation-variant inter-ensemble. The model's efficacy was validated across three benchmark datasets: AG-NEWS, IJCACT, IJCACT-TOYS, and the Reuters dataset. The results demonstrate that the proposed approach surpasses the performance of multiple state-of-the-art baselines, underscoring its efficacy.

We establish conditions and methodologies for meta-learning the successively higher-order linear representations of nonlinear functions, demonstrating that our approach enables the provably reliable recovery of the original functions from their respective learned representations. While our framework is grounded in linear representation theory, we specifically illustrate its application to neural networks utilizing ReLU activations. We validate our representation and learning theorems empirically through experiments on Gaussian mixture classification and distance metric learning.

Although machine translation (MT) has made significant strides in recent years, most current models remain too heavy for deployment in environments with limited computational resources. To create more efficient and light-weight alternatives, researchers have explored techniques such as network quantization and distillation, yet their impacts on MT model performance remain unclear. This study investigates the stability of these adaptive techniques—specifically quantization and distillation—across various evaluation metrics to assess their stability. Our findings indicate that these methods exhibit varying degrees of instability, which can result in suboptimal models. Consequently, we propose a systematic evaluation framework to guide practitioners in selecting the most appropriate method for low-resource MT model deployment.

The problem of determining whether a specific Lagrangian submanifold is Hamiltonian isotopic to a standard one is generally decidable, with a known procedure to compute, if a non-isotopic state exists, the shortest chain of moves required for this certification. This method relies on calculating move lengths using cohomology invariants, which are derived from counting solutions to certain virtual equations involving Hamiltonian symplections. We apply this general framework to demonstrate that, for single-hypergraph manifolds, these lengths correspond to sums of absolute values of the roots of certain polynomials. Furthermore, we show that these polynomials yield irreducible coefficients when expressed over the rational numbers, implying that, for single-hypergraph manifolds, these lengths cannot be rational numbers.

Segmentation serves as a crucial technique for identifying and segmenting organs or abnormalities within medical images, and accurate detection of pneumonia in chest X-rays holds significant value for clinical practice. This study introduces a novel approach leveraging data augmentation to lower data bias and enhance the performance of segmentation models, specifically for identifying pneumonia cases. By applying unsupervised pre-training on limited training datasets enriched with augmented samples generated from fully labeled sets, the model effectively captures robust features. These enriched datasets and associated strategies were evaluated against baseline methods using established benchmarks, specifically the two pneumonia chest X-ray collections (CheXNET and CAPD). Results indicate that the proposed technique surpasses models trained solely on smaller datasets by 1.5% on the higher difficulty ChexN dataset (reaching an 89.9% IoU) and the existing best method on the CAPD dataset (reaching a 79.1% IoU).

Image captioning is a natural language generation task that involves describing visual content. While recent advancements in image captioning have largely focused on improving accuracy, generating captions that satisfy additional constraints—such as controlling the tone or specific attributes of a caption—remains a less explored area. Addressing this, we propose a new approach called Controllable Image Captioning (CIC) using prompting. We achieve this by training a single model using a few-shot approach, where the model learns from examples within a prompt that specify both the requirements and the expected outputs. Extensive experiments on standard datasets demonstrate that our method is highly competitive compared to other state-of-the-art solutions. Furthermore, we introduce a new dataset that separates image requirements into distinct constraint categories, enabling more rigorous evaluation of controllable captioning models.

This work offers a novel perspective on defining harmful actions by integrating recent advancements in causal inference. We introduce a new formalization for establishing causality that accommodates both direct and indirect effects of an activity. Utilizing this framework, we present a unified analytical method for determining harm that applies equally to scenarios involving predefined outcomes and those that must be explicitly chosen by the recipient of the action. Finally, we demonstrate that our approach successfully unifies various existing definitions of harm while providing a robust theoretical foundation for future research and development in this critical area.

This study introduces MMLSpark, a scalable deep learning framework built on Microsoft's Spark for processing massive datasets. Designed to simplify model creation, it offers interfaces for both neural network consumers and specialists. The framework utilizes ScalaPy, a bespoke library enabling efficient manipulation of massive data structures. We evaluate various architectures—including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), and Transformer models—across computer vision and natural language processing tasks. Experimental results indicate optimal performance across tested workloads when a specialized batch processing approach is paired with optimized tensor structures in MMLSpark.

Speech translation involves converting spoken audio directly into written text or speech in another language. Conversely, zero-shot speech recognition transcribes audio into a language that was not present during the training phase. This research introduces a unified framework for zero-shot speech translation and zero-shot transcription, where transcription is defined as the English equivalent. By leveraging large-scale multilingual datasets, the proposed method generates language-specific decoders that allow a single shared encoder to handle audio from various languages effectively. Extensive experiments on speech-from-speech tasks across multiple language pairs demonstrate that this approach achieves state-of-the-art performance for zero-shot transcription and establishes a robust new baseline for zero-shot speech translation.

This abstract introduces a Coleman-Gurtin model featuring dynamic boundary conditions. The corresponding initial and boundary value problems within this framework are analyzed, specifically under scenarios where the model parameters are positive. A fundamental step of the investigation involves establishing regularity properties for the associated linear operator along with the existence of a unique strong solution to the associated linear problem. Leveraging these findings, the study demonstrates the existence and uniqueness of a weak solution for the non-linear model. Ultimately, an existence result for a strong solution is also provided.

Accurate short-term energy consumption forecasting is essential for the widespread adoption of energy storage and electric vehicles, particularly within low-voltage grids where daily peak demands dictate the size of local capacity expansions. This work presents an advanced probabilistic load forecasting framework specifically for single-day ahead prediction in low-voltage environments. The model is constructed using an innovative data fusion strategy that integrates both household-level and aggregate level load measurements to generate confidence intervals, which are quantified via discrete Bayesian updating of an initial probability density function. The study evaluates two distinct approaches: a traditional method relying on weighted Gaussian distributions and a cutting-edge technique based on Gaussian processes. The proposed fusion method is assessed on real-world datasets from Germany, demonstrating that incorporating granular household data significantly enhances both the accuracy and reliability of the resulting predictions.

Recent advancements in data analytics and machine learning have enabled the creation of increasingly complex and powerful models. However, a critical limitation remains: as models become more sophisticated, extracting their explanations and understanding their inner workings grow significantly more difficult. This challenge is compounded by the lack of accessible data on model behavior and performance, creating a closed feedback loop. Consequently, acquiring and explaining model functionality is more feasible when built using modern techniques like Neural Architecture Search (NAS). This approach allows for the systematic integration of domain expertise into machine learning models by defining problem-solving strategies within specific knowledge domains, such as image processing, and then employing optimization algorithms to build solutions aligned with that domain-specific insight. By facilitating the collaborative interaction between machine learning and domain experts, NAS enables the construction of models that satisfy diverse user requirements.

The ongoing global spread of the novel coronavirus (COVID-19) has caused massive loss of life and significant economic disruption. As a highly contagious respiratory illness, COVID-19 requires timely diagnosis and effective treatment to mitigate further transmission. While medical imaging, particularly chest CT scans, has proven effective for detecting the virus, the need for highly accurate and reliable algorithms is urgent. However, developing such methods presents a significant hurdle: the extreme scarcity of CT scans with confirmed COVID-19 labels. To address this limitation, the proposed approach employs a weakly supervised framework to train a lesion localization and segmentation system using only data annotated at the image level. This method eliminates dependency on expensive and time-consuming pixel-level annotations. The efficacy of this solution was evaluated on 1,050 chest CT images, and the experimental results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other state-of-the-art techniques.

Accurate localization and identification of vertebral bodies are essential for diagnosing various spine diseases. This study introduces a novel deep learning-based approach designed to detect and identify these structures within complex three-dimensional chest and abdominal CT volumes. Since deep learning models for segmentation typically struggle with objects of varying sizes, we first localize each vertebral body and then re-crop the surrounding context to standard relative dimensions, thereby enhancing detection consistency. Furthermore, accurate identification depends heavily on precise localization; to address irregularities and missing data, we rectify CT slices into their anatomical positions. This is achieved using an anatomically constrained optimization process that aligns the image with a predefined 2D vertebra template. With the slice properly aligned, we apply a pre-trained deep learning system for localization and identification. Finally, to ensure anatomical plausibility, we refine both the segmentation masks and identification labels by integrating constraints from a 3D vertebral template. Experimental results indicate that this end-to-end framework significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving a mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.62 mm in localization and a mean classification error of 0.04.

We present the first experimental verification of dynamical stabilization through response function analysis of electron scattering within a cavity, achieved by measuring the auto-correlation of cavity field intensity during resonant electron scattering. This process occurs under the extreme conditions of the ultrastrong light-matter regime, where a quantum emitter is driven by resonant electron scattering. Under these conditions, the incoming electron couples strongly to the system, and the dynamic instability caused by strong coupling is counteracted by dynamical stabilization, allowing the quantum emitter to persist. This work provides novel insights into the complex interactions between light and matter at the quantum level.

While spring-based elastic actuators have driven significant advancements in biological-inspired locomotion, engineering the optimal spring parameters remains difficult due to complex, non-linear dynamics. We introduce a machine learning approach designed to guide these parameters automatically, enabling the optimization of physical robot traits like mass and actuator placement. The method employs a hybrid representation that merges a simplified simulation model with machine learning predictions to forecast dynamics efficiently. The resulting learned landscape allows for the high-speed optimization of biologically and practically feasible configurations, significantly outperforming conventional control strategies tested on both a soft-spring prototype and the Unitree Go1 hard robot. The optimized design features versatile mass and actuator elasticity, facilitating agile real-world behaviors such as jumping, gaits transitions, and whole-body vibration.

We introduce the variational separability ansatz for quantum circuits, which is adaptable to the development of both approximate and exact separability algorithms across various quantum computing models. The efficacy of these ansatz methods relies on the circuits' capacity to effectively approximate the eigenvectors corresponding to the lowest eigenvalues of the separability Hamiltonian. Consequently, this allows for the formulation of both Lagrangian and Lagrangian-like optimization algorithms that can be executed using standard variational techniques. Additionally, the proposed framework is versatile enough to incorporate any existing separability Hamiltonian, thereby extending its applicability to a broad range of different problems.

This work examines the evolution of small-scale tearing modes in slab geometries within collisionless plasmas, specifically analyzing the initial setup, intermediate stages, and final states. The analysis begins by employing the adiabatic approximation to derive the equilibrium current profile, which allows for the identification of tearing mode rational surfaces. The intermediate phase is modeled using the thin-resistivity approach, where the dynamics are captured by a generalized island evolution equation that accounts for kinetic effects at the core of the magnetic island. The analysis concludes by employing a two-fluid framework to describe the final equilibrium, which incorporates the influence of a non-Maxwellian particle distribution. The findings are benchmarked against numerical simulations, demonstrating that the multi-scale framework accurately captures the essential physics of tearing mode development in collisionless plasmas.

This article addresses feature-level attribute modification in fashion imagery, specifically focusing on altering attribute values within a given image to generate a new representation. We introduce a novel Semi-supervised Attribute Manipulation (SAM) framework, which exploits a label dataset to train an attribute modifier. This modifier operates at the feature space, ensuring high-quality output images even when paired with unseen or sparse data at the image level. By effectively leveraging data from the label domain, our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, which are hindered by limited data availability. Extensive experiments on two prominent fashion retrieval benchmarks confirm the superiority of our SAM framework.

We present a cost construction technique for light field depth estimation that makes comprehensive use of all available data from a given light field. By combining two complementary approaches— a "local" constructor utilizing spatially adjacent pixels in the view with the largest aperture, and a "global" constructor relying on the view with the highest occlusion awareness— a cost volume is generated. This system ensures that the advantages of each individual view are preserved while mitigating occlusion artifacts. Experiments using a state-of-the-art structured-from-motion network demonstrate that the proposed method yields significant improvements in light field depth estimation accuracy.
